meta.blurb: London, May 1914. Richard Hannay is bored until a frightened neighbour tells him of a plot, and is then found dead. Hunted by police and spies, Hannay runs for the Scottish hills with a coded notebook. Can he decode it before it is too late?
meta.bible: Richard Hannay: a Scottish-born mining engineer, home from Rhodesia, brave, practical and quick-witted; the hero. Scudder: an American neighbour in Hannay's building who knows of a plot; he is found dead. Karolides: the Greek prime minister, due to visit London on 15 June. The Black Stone: a secret group of German spies working to steal British war plans. The Professor: the bald, polite leader of the Black Stone, whose eyelids close like a hawk's. Sir Harry: a young politician in Scotland who hides Hannay. Sir Walter Bullivant: a senior official at the Foreign Office. Inspector Scaife: a Scotland Yard detective. Royer: a French general who visits London for the secret meeting. Trafalgar Lodge: the villains' house on the Kent coast near Bradgate; thirty-nine steps lead from it down to the sea. Ariadne: the spies' yacht, due at high tide at seventeen minutes past ten in the evening. Galloway: the wild moorland of south-west Scotland. Rhodesia, London, Scotland, Scotland Yard, Foreign Office, Kent, Germany, France, Britain, Africa, American, Greek, German, French. Voice and tone: fast, plain and tense, a chase told with dry humour; a death is stated plainly with no gore; Hannay tells the story as a man who is not a hero by trade.

B1B2: Richard Hannay has come home from Africa with plenty of money, but London bores him badly. After three months in the city, he wishes he were back in the sun.
One evening a thin, frightened man knocks at Hannay's door. He is Scudder, an American who lives on the same floor, and he asks to come in.
Scudder tells him that Karolides, the Greek prime minister, will be killed in London on 15 June. The murder, he says, will push the great nations of Europe into war.
Scudder says the plot belongs to a secret group of spies called the Black Stone. They have found out that he knows, and they are watching the building.
Hannay decides that nobody could act such fear, and he offers Scudder a bed. For several days the little man stays inside and writes in a black notebook.
One evening Hannay comes home and finds Scudder lying dead on the floor of the sitting room. A long knife has been used, and the killer is gone.
Looking from the window, Hannay sees two men watching the street. He understands that the police will blame him, because he cannot explain the strange story to them.
Before dawn Hannay waits for the milkman who delivers to the building. He pays him well for his cap and white coat, and the man laughs and agrees.
Hannay walks down the steps and straight past the two men who are watching the door. They hardly look at him, and in a minute he has turned the corner and is free.
Hannay buys a ticket to the wild south-west of Scotland and takes the first train north. In the newspapers he reads that the police are already looking for him.
In Galloway the moors are wide and empty, and there are few people to ask questions. Hannay decides to hide there until 15 June and then find Sir Walter Bullivant.
At night Hannay works on the notebook, which is full of numbers, and he finds the key to the code. He learns that the plot is bigger than one murder.
At a small inn Hannay meets an innkeeper who loves adventure stories, and he is given a bed. The man asks few questions, and Hannay is glad of it.
Late at night two strangers arrive at the inn and ask about a tall man with a notebook. Hannay hears them from his room and climbs out of the window.
In a small village Hannay meets Sir Harry, a young politician, who takes him for a speaker he has been waiting for. Hannay is too tired to argue, and he agrees.
Hannay stands up and, to his own surprise, gives a lively speech that makes the audience laugh and cheer. Sir Harry listens, amazed, from the chair beside him on the stage.
Late that night Hannay tells Sir Harry the whole story, from Scudder's visit to the night of the milkman. To his relief, the young man believes every word.
In the morning Sir Harry gives Hannay a better suit and a map of the hills. He promises that he will tell the police nothing, and Hannay thanks him warmly.
On the road Hannay meets a roadmender who wears spectacles and breaks stones for a living. The man talks pleasantly, but his eyes rest too long on Hannay's good boots.
Later that day a small aeroplane appears over the hills and flies low above the road. It circles back, and Hannay is sure that it is searching for him.
Hannay throws himself into the heather beside a stream and lies perfectly still. The aeroplane passes over twice, and then it lands on the far side of the valley.
Hannay spends the whole night walking away from the aeroplane across the hills. He has no food, and by morning he is tired, wet and hungry.
At last Hannay finds a lonely house, and a bald, gentle old man invites him inside. He says he studies the remains of old buildings, and he offers hot food.
Hannay tells the old man a little of his story, and the host listens with great interest. That evening two more men arrive at the house, and they too seem very friendly.
Hannay sees the old man's eyelids slide over his eyes like a hawk's, just as Scudder said. In that moment he knows that he has walked straight into the enemy's house.
The three men take Hannay's coat and lock him in a small room. Hannay hears them talking in low voices outside, and he knows that he must escape quickly.
Searching the room, Hannay finds a box on a shelf that is full of explosives for the old man's digging. He thinks of a daring plan to blow open the door.
Hannay lights the fuse and hides behind a heavy table, and the door is thrown from its hinges with a great noise. In the smoke and confusion, he runs from the house.
Hannay runs across the moor until the sky begins to turn grey, and the house is far behind him. He is safe for now, but he has lost his bag and his food.
By a stream Hannay meets a quiet fisherman who shares his lunch with him. He also tells Hannay that a great meeting will be held in London on 15 June.
Late in the evening Hannay reaches the grand house of Sir Walter Bullivant. A servant lets him in, and soon he stands before a grey-haired man in a study.
Hannay tells Sir Walter the whole story from beginning to end. The older man listens without a word, and at last he nods slowly.
Sir Walter tells Hannay that Scudder had worked for the government and was one of their cleverest men. He says that he is sorry Scudder was killed, but that Hannay's story is true.
Sir Walter explains that the real danger is not a murder but a theft. A French general will come to London to talk of secret war plans, and the spies hope to steal them.
The 15th of June arrives, and General Royer meets the British officers in a secret room. Hannay waits with Sir Walter, and nothing seems to go wrong.
Hannay asks for a book of tide tables and looks through them carefully. At last he finds a harbour where high tide is at seventeen minutes past ten on one near evening.
Sir Walter fetches an old naval officer, and together they look at the map of the coast. The sailor points to a house called Trafalgar Lodge, near the town of Bradgate.
Inspector Scaife of Scotland Yard arrives and listens to the story with a serious face. To Hannay's surprise, he sees that the young man is honest and agrees to help him.
The three men get into a fast car and drive south-east through the lanes of Kent. They arrive near Bradgate as the sun is going down.
At last they come to Trafalgar Lodge, a neat white house on a high cliff above the sea. It looks quiet and ordinary, and a light is shining in one window.
On the lawn three men in white clothes are playing tennis and laughing together. They seem perfectly harmless, and Scaife begins to doubt Hannay's story.
Hannay looks closely at the oldest player and recognises him at once. He is the bald, gentle professor who locked him in the room on the moor, although he now wears white clothes.
While the others talk, Hannay walks to the edge of the garden and finds a wooden stair going down the cliff. He counts the steps carefully, and there are exactly thirty-nine.
Out in the bay Hannay sees a white yacht at anchor with a light at her mast. Her name is Ariadne, and a small boat is moving slowly across the dark water towards the beach.
Hannay runs to Scaife and tells him that the yacht has come. The police, who were waiting nearby, surround the three men before they can leave the garden.
The old man, calm to the last, looks at Hannay and says, in perfect English, that the game is up. He admits that the three of them are spies, and he asks for nothing.
Another group of police take the little boat as it lands on the beach. Soon the yacht Ariadne is stopped too, and no one escapes.
In the house the police find the copied war plans and a store of papers. Sir Walter looks at them carefully and tells Hannay that the danger has passed.
In August war comes to Europe, as Scudder feared, and Hannay decides to join the army. He knows now that the plans he saved will help his country.
Looking back, Hannay thinks about the strange weeks that began with a frightened man at his door. He is glad that he took the chance, and he never feels bored again.
C1C2: In the spring of 1914, Richard Hannay, a mining engineer who had spent years under the hot sun of Rhodesia, sat in his London flat and found the whole city unbearably dull. He had money enough and nothing to spend it on, and the dinners and clubs that other men enjoyed seemed to him a long grey waiting room. That evening he decided that, unless something happened soon, he would take the next ship back to Africa.

One evening, as Hannay was thinking about dinner, a thin and anxious man tapped softly at his door and slipped inside before he could answer. It was Scudder, an American who lived on the same floor and whom Hannay knew only by sight, a clever little fellow with a quick tongue. That night, however, his face was grey with fear, and his hands shook as he locked the door behind him.

Scudder confessed, in a low and hurried voice, that he had discovered a conspiracy to murder Karolides, the Greek prime minister, when he came to London on 15 June. The killing, he explained, was meant to set the nations of Europe quarrelling until the whole continent was drawn into war. Hannay, who had been prepared to think him a fantasist, found that the little man spoke with a calm that was far more convincing than any shouting.

The conspirators, Scudder went on, called themselves the Black Stone, and they were clever, patient men who served a foreign power and stopped at nothing. One of them, he warned, could be known by his eyelids, which closed over his eyes like those of a hawk, and that man would never forget a face. Already they had learned of his discoveries, he said, and he had not dared to sleep in his own rooms for three nights.

Something in the man's terror persuaded Hannay that he was neither a madman nor a liar, and he offered his spare room without another question. For several days Scudder stayed indoors, scribbling in a small black notebook and starting at every sound on the stairs. Hannay, who had never before been so useful to anyone, discovered to his surprise that he was rather enjoying himself.

When Hannay returned from dinner one evening, he found the door unlocked and Scudder lying dead upon the floor of the sitting room. A long knife had been driven through his heart, and the killers, whoever they were, had left without disturbing anything else. For a few moments Hannay could only stand and stare, while the clock on the mantelpiece ticked on as calmly as ever.

Peering cautiously through the curtains, Hannay noticed two idle figures loitering on the pavement opposite, their eyes fixed on his door. It dawned on him that the police would soon find a dead man in his flat, and that no jury would believe a story about spies and a hawk-eyed stranger. He picked up Scudder's notebook, which lay open on the table, and slipped it inside his coat.

Before dawn, Hannay waited in the shadows of the staircase until the milkman came whistling up the steps with his cans. A few coins and a story about a joke on a friend were enough to buy the man's blue cap and long white coat, and the milkman, who was easily amused, went off cheerfully in his shirtsleeves. A minute later Hannay was dressed as an ordinary tradesman, with a can in each hand.

Carrying his cans with the easy swing of a man who had done the round every morning of his life, Hannay stepped out into the grey street and strolled directly past the watchers. One of them glanced at him for an instant, yawned, and turned back to the house, and no one suspected that the wanted man was whistling a milkman's tune. Once he had rounded the corner, he dropped the cans in a doorway and quickened his pace.

Hannay judged that the surest place to vanish was the loneliest, and so he bought a ticket for the wild moorland of Galloway and caught the first train northward. Somewhere beyond the English border he unfolded a newspaper and found his own description, with a reward for information about the man wanted for Scudder's murder. He pulled his cap lower over his face and watched the green hills roll by.

Galloway proved to be a country of long brown hills, lonely farms and winding roads where a stranger might walk for hours without meeting a soul. Hannay resolved to hide there for the best part of a month, and then, before 15 June, to find Sir Walter Bullivant, the one man whom Scudder had said could be trusted. Until that day came, his only business was to stay alive, keep out of sight, and trust nobody at all.

By candlelight in a shepherd's empty hut, Hannay puzzled over the notebook's columns of numbers until, after many hours, the key to Scudder's cipher came suddenly clear. What he read astonished him, for the planned killing of Karolides was little more than a decoy, and the true aim of the Black Stone was the theft of Britain's secret plans for war. Beside one entry, written in Scudder's neat hand, stood three mysterious words, thirty-nine steps, followed by a puzzling time, high tide, seventeen minutes past ten.

At a small inn beside the road, Hannay met an innkeeper who read detective stories in every spare moment and was delighted to shelter a mysterious stranger. He asked remarkably few questions, perhaps because he suspected the answers would be more thrilling than any book on his shelf. Hannay slept that night in a real bed for the first time since leaving London.

Late the next evening, two hard-faced strangers arrived at the inn and began asking whether a tall, brown-faced man had lodged there. Hannay, listening on the stairs, knew by instinct that they were no policemen, and as soon as they sat down to supper he climbed out of his window and dropped quietly onto the grass. By the time they looked for him he was a mile away in the darkness.

In a small village Hannay stumbled upon a young politician named Sir Harry, who mistook him for the speaker he had been anxiously awaiting that evening. Too worn out to argue and in need of a roof, Hannay allowed the mistake to continue and was hurried into a hall already filling with farmers and shopkeepers. It was, he reflected with some amusement, a very odd way for a man hunted by the police to hide himself from the world.

Hannay rose before the crowd, cleared his throat, and began to speak on whatever came into his head, which turned out to be a great deal of plain common sense mixed with jokes about the weather. The audience laughed and clapped, and by the end of the evening they were cheering him as if he had been a politician all his life. Sir Harry, who had been dreading a dull and empty meeting, sat beside him and could hardly believe his good luck.

When the crowd had gone home, Hannay told Sir Harry the whole truth, beginning with Scudder's frightened visit and ending with the knife, the milkman and the long flight north. Sir Harry listened with wide eyes and, to Hannay's great relief, declared that no man could invent such a tale and that he would help in any way he could. After weeks of running and lying, it was the first honest kindness that Hannay had received from a living soul.

In the morning Sir Harry produced a decent tweed suit, a good map of the hills, and a promise that no policeman would hear a word from him about the stranger who had spoken in the hall. Hannay thanked him warmly, folded the map into his pocket, and went out into the morning feeling a stranger and much less hunted. He did not yet know how short a time that comfortable feeling was going to last, nor what was waiting beyond the next hill.

Walking along a quiet road beside a hillside, Hannay fell into conversation with a roadmender in thick spectacles, who sat in the sun breaking stones into neat piles. The man was pleasant enough, and yet there was something wrong about the way his eyes lingered upon Hannay's boots, which were far too good for a wandering labourer. Hannay felt, with a sudden chill, that he was being studied as carefully as a specimen, and he rose, said good day, and walked on.

Late in the afternoon a small aeroplane droned out of the south and swept low over the road, turned in a slow circle, and came back again. In the empty hills there was nothing for it to find but a single walking man, and Hannay knew with perfect certainty that the machine was looking for him. He stood still for one cold moment, with the sun in his eyes and the engine growling overhead, and then he began to run.

He flung himself down in the thick heather beside a stream and lay motionless, his face pressed against the cool earth, while the engine roared twice above his head. At last the machine landed on a flat field across the valley, and Hannay could see two figures climbing out and looking about them with field glasses. He crept away along the stream on his belly until they were hidden by the hill.

Throughout the night he tramped across hill and bog, guided only by the stars, putting as many miles as he could between himself and his pursuers. By dawn he was hungry, drenched to the knees and aching in every limb, but the thought that he had slipped through their fingers once more kept him moving. He promised himself a hot meal, a fire and a dry pair of socks at the very first house that he found.

At the end of a long track he found a lonely house with smoke rising from its chimney, and a pleasant, bald old gentleman who welcomed him in as though visitors were a rare treat. The old man explained that he was an archaeologist who studied ruins and the remains of ancient camps, and he ordered a hot breakfast for the exhausted stranger. Hannay, grateful for the kindness and far too weary to be careful, sat down at the old man's table and ate like a starving soldier.

Over a long dinner, Hannay told the kindly old man a carefully edited version of his adventures, and the host listened with an interest that was almost too keen. Towards evening two more men arrived at the house, both polite and smiling, and they greeted the bald gentleman like an old friend. Hannay felt a faint unease which he could not quite explain, although nothing in the pleasant talk gave him a reason to be afraid.

As the old man lowered his gaze to the table, his eyelids slid slowly across his eyes with a motion exactly like that of a hawk, and Hannay remembered Scudder's warning with a shock that ran down his spine. Here, in the quiet house on the moor, sat the very man who commanded the Black Stone, and Hannay had told him half of his secrets over dinner. The polite smile that followed, calm and patient and perfectly friendly, seemed to Hannay more menacing than any shouted threat could have been.

Without a word of threat, the three men seized Hannay, took his coat, and locked him in a small room at the back of the house. Through the keyhole he could hear them talking in low, serious voices, and it was plain that they were deciding his fate. If he stayed where he was until morning, Hannay told himself, he would never see another sunrise.

Searching every corner of his prison, Hannay discovered on a high shelf a wooden box of explosives, which the old man evidently used for his excavations. The discovery made him smile for the first time in hours, for it gave him a chance at freedom that no locked door could prevent. With the greatest care he began to set a small charge against the hinges.

He lit the fuse, crouched behind a heavy oak table, and waited, counting the seconds, until the whole room shuddered with a deafening roar. The door was torn from its hinges, and while the startled spies rushed about in smoke and darkness, Hannay leapt through the wreckage and out into the night. Behind him he could hear shouting, but nobody dared to follow him into the blackness.

He ran across the moor until his lungs burned and the first grey light was showing in the east, by which time the house was nothing but a dark shape in the distance. The spies would doubtless search for him in the hills, but for the moment he was free, hungry and without a single belonging except what he wore. The notebook, he was glad to discover as he stopped to catch his breath, was still safe in the inner pocket of his coat.

By a bright stream Hannay came upon a quiet man in a floppy hat, patiently casting a fly, who cheerfully shared his lunch with a stranger and asked no questions at all. From him Hannay gathered a little news, among it the interesting fact that an important meeting of officers was expected in London in mid-June. It confirmed what the notebook had hinted, and he thanked the fisherman more warmly than the sandwiches deserved.

Late in the evening, dusty and unshaven, Hannay reached the great house of Sir Walter Bullivant and, after some arguing with a suspicious servant, was shown into a book-lined study. There he was received by a grey-haired, courteous gentleman who looked at him as though he had been expecting him for some time. It was the first moment in many long days when Hannay allowed himself to hope that his troubles might actually be coming to an end.

Speaking steadily, Hannay recounted every detail of his adventures, from the first knock at his door to the explosion in the old man's house, while Sir Walter listened without once interrupting. At the end of the account the great man nodded slowly, took the notebook, and examined it for a long time under the lamp. His grave face suggested that he had heard something very much more serious than a tale of murder.

Sir Walter then explained that Scudder had in fact been working in secret for the government, and that he had been one of the cleverest and bravest men in the whole service. He regretted his death bitterly, he said, but it proved that Scudder had been right to fear, and it confirmed that every word of Hannay's tale was true. It was, for a man who had been hunted as a murderer for weeks, a profound and almost overwhelming relief to be believed at last.

The real danger, Sir Walter explained, was not the death of Karolides but the theft of the secret plans by which Britain and France intended to defend themselves in a war. A French general named Royer was about to visit London to discuss those plans with senior officers, and the Black Stone meant to copy them and carry them out of the country. The assassination story, he said, had been a clever mask over a far more serious design.

On the fifteenth of June the French general met the British officers in a closely guarded room, and the great plan was discussed in complete secrecy. Hannay waited at Sir Walter's side, expecting at any moment to hear that the spies had struck, but the hours passed without an alarm. It was the very silence that troubled him, for the Black Stone was not a group that gave up easily.

Hannay borrowed a book of tide tables and ran his finger down the columns until he found a harbour on the south-east coast where high water fell at seventeen minutes past ten on the evening of the following day. The coincidence was too neat to ignore, and he reflected that spies who wished to leave the country by sea would naturally choose a night when the tide could carry them out. The deadline, it seemed, was not weeks away as he had feared but a matter of a few short hours, and there was no time to lose.

Sir Walter summoned an old naval officer who knew the south-eastern coast intimately, and the three men bent together over a large map spread across the study table. The sailor laid a finger upon a small house called Trafalgar Lodge, perched on a cliff near the town of Bradgate, and declared that a steep stair of wooden steps led down from its garden to the beach. Hannay's heart began to beat faster as he realised that the words in the notebook might at last be pointing to a real and definite place.

Inspector Scaife of Scotland Yard arrived at the house the same night, and Hannay braced himself for arrest, since the man had been hunting him for weeks. Instead, after hearing the story and examining the notebook, the Inspector looked at Hannay with grudging respect and agreed that the matter must be investigated at once. A wanted man, Hannay reflected, had never been so happy to meet a policeman.

They set out in a fast motor car, Hannay and the Inspector beside the driver, and sped through the narrow lanes of Kent as the afternoon faded into evening. By the time the first stars appeared they were close to the sea, and the smell of salt hung in the cool air. Hannay felt the tension of a man about to cross a line from which there was no turning back.

At last they came to Trafalgar Lodge, a neat white house on a cliff top, with a trim garden in front and the grey sea stretching away behind. Nothing about it suggested villainy, and a light burned peacefully in an upper window, but Hannay was certain that the house held the answer to the whole mystery. They left the car in a lane and walked the last few hundred yards.

On the lawn behind the house three men in white flannels were playing tennis in the last of the light, laughing and calling out the score like any group of friends. They looked so thoroughly respectable that Inspector Scaife began to murmur doubts, and even Hannay, for an instant, wondered whether he had made a terrible mistake. Then the eldest of the three turned his face towards the sea, and the last of the evening light fell full upon it.

Hannay looked hard at the eldest of the three and knew him instantly, in spite of the changed clothes and a different manner of standing. It was the gentle, bald archaeologist from the moorland house, the man who had shut him in the room full of explosives, and the slow droop of his eyelids was unmistakable. Hannay turned to the Inspector and whispered that they had found the Black Stone.

While the Inspector argued politely with the three men, Hannay wandered to the edge of the garden, where a steep wooden stair dropped away down the face of the cliff. He counted the steps as he went down them, one after another, and when he reached the shingle at the bottom, the number in his head was exactly thirty-nine. The riddle of the notebook was solved at last, and as he stood on the shingle he could hear the tide creeping steadily in.

Out in the bay, a white steam yacht rode at anchor with a lantern at her mast, and across the dark water a small boat was already beginning to pull towards the beach. Her name, which Hannay could just make out through the dusk, was Ariadne, and it was very nearly the moment for which the whole conspiracy had been designed. Understanding everything in a flash, Hannay turned and raced back up the thirty-nine steps with his heart thumping against his ribs.

Hannay burst into the garden crying that the yacht had come, and Inspector Scaife, convinced at last, blew his whistle for the policemen waiting in the lane. Before the three men could reach the cliff, the garden was full of uniformed officers, and the Professor and his friends were surrounded and seized without a struggle. Only the cold glitter of the old man's eyes, half hidden behind their heavy lids, revealed anything of what he was feeling.

The old man, still perfectly composed, turned his heavy-lidded gaze upon Hannay and remarked, in flawless English, that the game was lost and that he congratulated his opponent. He asked for nothing and denied nothing, and in that quiet admission, Hannay recognised the same dreadful patience that had murdered Scudder. It was the end of the Black Stone's greatest and most patient plan, and Hannay felt no triumph, only a heavy sort of quiet.

At the foot of the cliff, a second party of policemen seized the little boat as it ran up the shingle, and naval craft that had been warned in advance closed quietly around the Ariadne. Her crew, who had expected nothing worse than a quiet night's work, were taken without a shot being fired. Not a single page of the secret plans, whether original or copy, was to leave the shores of England that night or ever.

Inside Trafalgar Lodge the searchers found the copied plans spread upon a table, together with a quantity of letters and drawings that revealed the whole organisation of the Black Stone. Sir Walter examined them one by one, and then he turned to Hannay with the quiet remark that a very serious danger had been averted. It was, he said gravely, a night that the nation would never hear about, though it would owe a great deal to it.

In August the war that Scudder had feared broke over Europe at last, and Hannay, with a clear conscience and a pair of strong hands, joined the army without a moment's hesitation. He knew that the secret plans he had helped to protect would serve his comrades well, and he felt neither fear nor regret. The restless boredom that had weighed upon him in the grey London spring had vanished for ever, and he never felt it again.

Looking back later on the strange weeks that had begun with a knock at the door, Hannay marvelled at how closely safety and danger had walked together. A bored man in a quiet flat had been drawn, step by step, into a struggle that might have changed the course of a war, and he was grateful for every moment of it. Whenever he saw a long flight of stairs, he smiled and remembered the thirty-nine steps.
